ALPHABET = '123456789ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijkmnopqrstuvwxyz'
def b58(data):
    n = int.from_bytes(data, 'big')
    out = ''
    while n:
        n, r = divmod(n, 58)
        out = ALPHABET[r] + out
    zeros = len(data) - len(data.lstrip(b'\x00'))
    return '1' * zeros + out

title: Mining and Consensus

nodes.label: Money creation
nodes.body: The first subject is the way new coins come into being: a reward that is cut in half on a fixed timetable and the fees of the transactions, claimed in the first transaction of each block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Each statement was recomputed from the code and the real halving blocks, and the reward rules were tried on a private chain of Bitcoin Core 31.1 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This subject covers Subsidy schedule; Reward composition.

nodes.label: Subsidy schedule
nodes.body: This section is about the timetable of the reward: the halving every 210,000 blocks, the limit on the supply, an error in the book's script and the shortened interval of regtest (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This subject covers Halving every 210,000 blocks; Total supply below 21 million; The float erratum of the book's script; Regtest halves every 150 blocks.

nodes.label: Halving every 210,000 blocks
nodes.body: The reward that a miner may claim in the first transaction of a block, the subsidy, starts at 50 coins and is cut in half every 210,000 blocks, which the book describes as about every four years (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the code it is one line, the subsidy is shifted right by the number of halvings, and the interval is a constant of the chain parameters (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Real blocks show the schedule: block 210,000 was mined on 2012-11-28 and pays 25 coins, block 420,000 on 2016-07-09 pays 12.5, block 630,000 on 2020-05-11 pays 6.25 and block 840,000 on 2024-04-20 pays 3.125, and the block before each one pays exactly twice as much (Mempool Space, 2026). It is like a fruit tree that bears half as much every four years on a fixed timetable: nobody votes on it, the calendar of blocks decides. This example reads mempool_block_210000.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.14.6 and not in your browser: ([(210000, '2012-11-28', 25.0, 50.0), (420000, '2016-07-09', 12.5, 25.0), (630000, '2020-05-11', 6.25, 12.5), (840000, '2024-04-20', 3.125, 6.25)], '210000', True)
nodes.definition: The subsidy is 50 coins shifted right by one bit for every 210,000 blocks: blocks 210,000, 420,000, 630,000 and 840,000 were mined on 2012-11-28, 2016-07-09, 2020-05-11 and 2024-04-20 and carry 25, 12.5, 6.25 and 3.125 coins, each half of the block before it, and the interval is the constant nSubsidyHalvingInterval of 210,000.

nodes.label: Total supply below 21 million
nodes.body: Because the subsidy is an integer number of satoshis that is halved by a shift, it reaches 1 satoshi in the thirty-third period and zero after that, so the total can be added up exactly (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The sum of all rewards is 2,099,999,997,690,000 satoshis, which is 2,310,000 satoshis, or 0.0231 coins, less than the round figure of 21 million coins; the last block that pays anything is block 6,929,999, and the book places the end of issuance in about the year 2140 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The small gap is rounding, since each halving drops the odd satoshi, and the Bitcoin Wiki states the same fixed supply as a necessary condition for a meaningful currency (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). It is like a savings jar into which a smaller and smaller number of coins is dropped each year until the last coin is a single cent: the jar never quite reaches the round figure on the label.
nodes.definition: Summing the 33 non-zero rewards in whole satoshis gives 2,099,999,997,690,000 satoshis, 2,310,000 satoshis (0.0231 coins) short of 21 million coins; the last block with a reward of 1 satoshi is 6,929,999 and block 6,930,000 has none, about the year 2140, because the code shifts an integer.

nodes.label: The float erratum of the book's script
nodes.body: The book prints a short script to add up all the rewards and shows the answer 2099999997690000 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The script that ships with the book divides the reward with current_reward /= 2 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); in Python 3 the slash is a float division, so the reward never reaches zero by halving to 1 satoshi and then 0, but goes on through fractions for 1,107 steps until the float underflows, and the script as printed gives 2100000000000000.0 and not the number of the book. With integer division, as the Bitcoin Core code does, the sum is again 2,099,999,997,690,000, which this chapter recomputed from both versions. It is like a baker who rounds every half loaf down to a whole loaf: with a calculator that keeps the half loaves forever you get a slightly different, and wrong, bill.
nodes.definition: The script max_money.py of the book divides the reward with current_reward /= 2, which is a float division in Python 3, so run as printed it goes on halving into fractions for 1,107 steps until the float underflows to zero and prints 2100000000000000.0 and not the 2099999997690000 of the book; with the integer division //= the result of the book appears.

nodes.label: Regtest halves every 150 blocks
nodes.body: A developer cannot wait four years to watch a halving, so the regtest chain halves every 150 blocks, a constant in the chain parameters (Bitcoin Core, 2026). On the Bitcoin Core 31.1 test chain the subsidy was 50 coins at heights 1 and 149, 25 at 150 and 299, 12.5 at 300 and 449 and 6.25 at 450, and at height 2,000 it had fallen to 610,351 satoshis, the value that the same shift rule gives (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book relies on this interval when it mines 500 blocks on regtest, and the test chain of this chapter reached height 2,101 within seconds because no real work is needed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like a flight simulator with the clock at fast forward: the controls are the real ones, only the hours are shortened.
nodes.definition: On regtest the halving interval is 150, so the test chain showed 50 coins at heights 1 and 149, 25 at 150 and 299, 12.5 at 300 and 449 and 6.25 at 450, and at height 2,000 the reward had shrunk to 610,351 satoshis, the value of the same shift rule.

nodes.label: Reward composition
nodes.body: This section is about what the reward is made of, the subsidy and the fees, and about the rule that the sum may be claimed in full, partly, but never above the limit (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This subject covers Reward is subsidy plus fees; The fees of block 840,000; Miner may claim less; Greedy coinbase rejected.

nodes.label: Reward is subsidy plus fees
nodes.body: The first transaction of a block, the coinbase, may create at most the subsidy plus the fees of all the other transactions of the block, a rule that the book explains with the miner who 'keeps the change' (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A block template of Bitcoin Core 31.1 on the test chain stated the sum in its coinbasevalue: 345,369 satoshis, made of 305,175 of subsidy and 40,194 of fees from four transactions (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The same sum holds on the real chain: block 277,316, the book's example, had a reward of 2,509,094,928 satoshis, 25 coins plus 9,094,928 satoshis of fees (Mempool Space, 2026). It is like the till at the end of the day: the new money printed for the shift plus the tips left on the tables is the most the waiter can take home. This example reads mempool_block_277316.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.14.6 and not in your browser: (345369, 345369, 40194, 2509094928, 2509094928, True)

nodes.label: The fees of block 840,000
nodes.body: The book says that fees are usually a small percentage of a miner's income, with the vast majority coming from the new coins (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Block 840,000, the first block to pay only 3.125 coins, which ViaBTC mined on 2024-04-20, held 3,050 transactions with fees of 3,762,561,499 satoshis, 37.6 coins, which is 12.04 times the subsidy of 312,500,000 satoshis (Mempool Space, 2026). That block was an exception, and the book's claim held for most blocks of its time, but it shows that the claim is not a law and that the share of fees can change from one block to the next, which fits the book's remark that fees will matter more as the reward decreases. It is like a restaurant where the tips on one holiday evening were twelve times the wage: unusual, but proof that the tips can matter. This example reads mempool_block_840000.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.14.6 and not in your browser: (3762561499, 312500000, 12.04, True, 'ViaBTC', 3050, True)

nodes.label: Miner may claim less
nodes.body: A rule that only caps the reward lets a miner take less than the cap, and the book notes that a miner may intentionally mine a block with less than the full reward, which lowers the total ever issued (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). On the test chain a block whose coinbase took 345,368 satoshis, one less than the 345,369 allowed, was accepted by the node; the satoshi that was not claimed never comes into existence (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Validation only compares the sum of the coinbase outputs with the limit, which the source of validation.cpp shows as a check for 'greater than' (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It is like a ceiling price on a market stall: the seller may sell below it, and nothing makes the stall owner charge the full amount.
nodes.definition: A miner may leave part of the reward unclaimed: on the test chain a block whose coinbase took 345,368 satoshis, one less than the allowed 345,369, was accepted, and the satoshi never exists, which is the 'lower total issuance' that the book mentions.

nodes.label: Greedy coinbase rejected
nodes.body: The cap is enforced by every node, not by trust: a coinbase that takes one satoshi more than subsidy plus fees makes the whole block invalid (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). On the test chain the node answered bad-cb-amount to a block that claimed 345,370 satoshis where 345,369 were allowed, and again to a hand-built block one satoshi above its limit, and the string bad-cb-amount appears in the source of validation.cpp (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The miner loses all the work spent on the block, since honest nodes ignore it, so cheating costs far more than the satoshi gained. It is like a cashier whose drawer is counted by every other cashier before the shift is accepted: one extra coin and the whole count is thrown out.

nodes.label: Decentralized consensus
nodes.body: The second subject is why nobody has to be trusted: every node checks every transaction and block by the same rules, picks the chain with the most work and rejects the rest (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Thirteen transaction cases and fourteen block cases were run against a Bitcoin Core 31.1 node (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This subject covers Independent verification; Chain selection.

nodes.label: Independent verification
nodes.body: This section is about the checklists: the transaction rules, the block rules and the maturity of rewards, each tested with a rule broken on purpose (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This subject covers Transaction checklist; Block checklist; Coinbase maturity.

nodes.label: Transaction checklist
nodes.body: Before a miner puts a transaction in a block, and before any node relays it, the node applies a fixed list of checks to it, which the book lists as the first part of independent verification (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). On the Bitcoin Core 31.1 test chain thirteen cases were run through testmempoolaccept: transactions with no outputs, a negative output, an output over 21 million coins, a total over 21 million coins, a repeated input, an input that does not exist, outputs larger than the inputs, a locktime in the future and a wrong signature were each refused with their own named reason, such as bad-txns-vout-empty or bad-txns-in-belowout, a transaction with no inputs could not be decoded at all, and a coinbase of depth 100 was allowed (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The names come from the rejection reasons in the source (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It is like the checks at an airport: ticket, passport, bag, each with its own reason for turning you back.

nodes.label: Block checklist
nodes.body: The same strictness is applied to a whole block, with a longer list of reasons, and a block that fails any one of them is thrown away by every node (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). For this chapter fourteen blocks were assembled byte by byte, each broken in one way, and submitted to a Bitcoin Core 31.1 node: a wrong merkle root (bad-txnmrklroot), no proof of work (high-hash), a time equal to the median (time-too-old), a time two hours and a second ahead (time-too-new), a reward one satoshi too high (bad-cb-amount), no height in the coinbase (bad-cb-height), a version of 1 (bad-version), wrong difficulty bits (bad-diffbits), coinbase scripts of 1 and 101 bytes (bad-cb-length), a second coinbase (bad-cb-multiple), a missing coinbase (bad-cb-missing) and a block over the weight limit (bad-blk-length), while the correct block was accepted (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The reasons are defined in the validation source of the node (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It is like a quality inspector with a clipboard of fourteen boxes: the product ships only when every box is ticked.

nodes.label: Coinbase maturity
nodes.body: A coinbase output cannot be spent until 100 blocks have been built on top of its block, a rule that the book states when it describes the first transaction of a block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The constant COINBASE_MATURITY is 100 in the consensus code (Bitcoin Core, 2026), and on the test chain a transaction spending a coinbase was refused with bad-txns-premature-spend-of-coinbase at depth 1 and at depth 99, and allowed at depth 100 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The delay protects everyone downstream: if the block that created the coins is replaced in a reorganization, the coins disappear with it, and nobody has yet received them. It is like a bank that holds a cheque for ten days before letting you draw on it, in case the cheque bounces.

nodes.label: Chain selection
nodes.body: This section is about choosing between competing chains by most work and about what happens to a payment when the chain that holds it is replaced (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This subject covers Most work, not longest; Double spend by reorganization.

nodes.label: Most work, not longest
nodes.body: When two valid chains compete, a node follows the one with the most cumulative proof of work, which the book defines as the best chain, rather than the one with the most blocks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the test the winning tip had the chainwork 208 against 206 for the chain it replaced; and when two blocks of equal work arrived at height 102, the node kept the first it had seen as its tip and marked the other valid-headers until more work arrived (Bitcoin Core, 2026). On regtest every block adds 2 units of work, so 208 is the work of the 104 blocks from the genesis block to height 103, and on the real chain a block with a harder target adds more work than an easier one (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It is like a tug of war decided by total pull and not by the number of pullers: one strong team beats two weak ones.
nodes.definition: Nodes follow the valid chain with the most cumulative work, not the one with the most blocks: after the test double spend the winning tip had chainwork 208 against 206, a tie in work (two blocks at height 102) left the first-seen block as the tip and the other as valid-headers, and the book states the rule as 'the most cumulative PoW'.

nodes.label: Double spend by reorganization
nodes.body: A payment is only as final as the chain that holds it, and the book shows how a double spend works: the buyer sends a competing transaction that spends the same coins and cancels the payment (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). On two Bitcoin Core 31.1 test nodes the payment of 49.999 coins to Carol was confirmed once and the wallet showed that she had received it; a competing branch that refunded the same coins to Mallory was then given one block more work, and the node reorganized, the payment showed -2 confirmations (a conflicted transaction), Carol had received 0 and the refund had 2 confirmations (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Rosenfeld's analysis of hashrate-based double spending gives the probability of such a reversal for attackers of every size (Rosenfeld, 2014). It is like a shop that hands over goods against a cheque, only to learn later that the bank has cancelled it: the more banks have countersigned, the less likely it is.
nodes.definition: In the test, Mallory's payment of 49.999 coins to Carol had 1 confirmation and Carol had received 49.999; then a competing block with a refund of the same coins was added with one block more of work, the payment went to -2 confirmations (conflicted), Carol had received 0 and the refund had 2 confirmations.

nodes.label: Building the candidate block
nodes.body: The third subject is how a miner assembles a block from the template, the coinbase and the header before any hashing is done (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The fields were read from real blocks of the main chain and from templates of a node (Mempool Space, 2026). This subject covers Block template; Coinbase transaction; Header construction.

nodes.label: Block template
nodes.body: This section is about the template that a node gives to a miner and the order in which it fills a block with transactions (Dashjr, 2012). This subject covers Template fields; Fee rate ordering.

nodes.label: Template fields
nodes.body: A miner does not build a block from nothing: the node hands over a template, a list of everything the miner needs except the work, through the RPC getblocktemplate that BIP 22 defines (Dashjr, 2012). The template of the Bitcoin Core 31.1 test chain at height 1 carried the hash of the parent, the height, the bits and the target, the current time and the earliest allowed time, the coinbasevalue of 5,000,000,000 satoshis, the limits weightlimit 4,000,000 and sigoplimit 80,000, the nonce range 00000000ffffffff, the active rules csv, segwit and taproot, and the default witness commitment (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book describes the same steps as building a candidate block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like a work order from a workshop: the foreman gives you the drawings, the material and the deadline, and you only add the labour.

nodes.definition: A block template gives the miner everything but the work: previousblockhash, height, bits and target, curtime and mintime, the coinbasevalue (5,000,000,000 satoshis at height 1), the limits weightlimit 4,000,000 and sigoplimit 80,000, the nonce range 00000000ffffffff, the rules csv, segwit and taproot, and the default witness commitment.

nodes.label: Fee rate ordering
nodes.body: A block has room for only 4,000,000 weight units, so a node fills the template with the transactions that pay the most for the room they take, measured as the fee rate in satoshis per virtual byte, as the chapter on fees explains (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). On the test chain four transactions paying 200, 50, 10 and 2 satoshis per virtual byte were placed in the mempool in the reverse order, and the node put them in the block in the order 200, 50, 10, 2 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The block assembler of release 31.1 adds the chunks of the mempool to the template in the order of their fee rate, and tests each chunk against the weight and signature-operation limits of the block (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It is like the last seats on an overbooked flight: the airline sells them first to the passengers who pay the most per kilo of luggage.
nodes.definition: Bitcoin Core fills a template from the mempool by fee rate: four transactions of 200, 50, 10 and 2 satoshis per virtual byte entered the block in exactly that order, the highest payer first.

nodes.label: Coinbase transaction
nodes.body: This section is about the first transaction of the block: its null input, the height, the locktime, the witness commitment, the tags and the extra nonce (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This subject covers Coinbase input is null; BIP 34 height push; Coinbase fields of Bitcoin Core today; Witness commitment; Coinbase data and tags; The extra nonce changes the root.

nodes.label: Coinbase input is null
nodes.body: The first transaction of every block, the coinbase, creates coins instead of moving them, so its single input spends nothing: the previous transaction hash is 32 zero bytes and the output index is ffffffff (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The coinbase of block 1 of the test chain, in the getblock output of Bitcoin Core 31.1, had exactly one input, a script of 5100, which is the height 1 followed by OP_0, and the sequence 4294967294 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). That script field is where the miner may write free data, and it must be 2 to 100 bytes long. It is like a bank note printed by the mint: it has no previous owner, only a serial number that says when it was printed.

nodes.label: BIP 34 height push
nodes.body: A coinbase has no input to make it unique, so two blocks could in theory have coinbases with the same identifier; BIP 34 closes the gap by requiring the block height as the first item in the coinbase script, written as a 'minimally encoded serialized CScript' number (Andresen, 2012). On the test chain the coinbase at height 2204 began 029c08, a push of two bytes holding 0x089c, which is 2204 in little-endian order, and the lines of chainparams.cpp fix the mainnet height at which the rule applies as 227,931 (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book lists the field as 'arbitrary data used for extra nonce and mining tags' and says that in version 2 blocks it must begin with the block height (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like numbering every cheque in a cheque book: even if the amount is the same, no two cheques have the same number. This example reads bip-0034.mediawiki, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.14.6 and not in your browser: ('029c08', '029c0800', 2204, True, '227931')
nodes.definition: Since BIP 34 the coinbase script begins with the block height as a minimally encoded number: height 2204 was written 029c08, a push of 2 bytes holding 0x089c in little-endian order, and the rule has been active on mainnet since block 227,931.

nodes.label: Coinbase fields of Bitcoin Core today
nodes.body: Bitcoin Core 31.1 fills in three details of the coinbase that the book does not mention: nLockTime is the height minus 1, nSequence is 0xfffffffe, and the script ends with OP_0 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The test coinbase at height 2204 had locktime 2203 and sequence 4294967294, and the coinbase of block 1 ended with the byte 00; the reason, given in BIP 54, is that a locktime tied to the height makes every new coinbase differ from the early violations of BIP 34, so that no coinbase can repeat a previous one (Poinsot and Corallo, 2025). The book's table of the coinbase lists only the input fields and the free data (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like the date stamped on a receipt by a modern till, a detail that an old manual describing receipts does not show.
nodes.definition: The coinbase transaction of Bitcoin Core 31.1 sets nLockTime to the height minus 1 and nSequence to 0xfffffffe, and ends its script with OP_0; the test coinbase at height 2204 had locktime 2203, and the book describes none of these fields.

nodes.label: Witness commitment
nodes.body: Segregated witness moved signatures out of the transaction identifier, so the block needed a new place to commit to them, and BIP 141 puts a hash in an output of the coinbase whose script begins 6a24aa21a9ed (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The 32 bytes that follow are the double SHA-256 of the witness merkle root and a 32-byte reserved value of zeros; the test chain's template gave the script, and an independent computation from the five witness transaction identifiers, with the coinbase counted as 32 zero bytes, gave the same commitment as the block (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book describes the merkle tree of witness identifiers and the 32 zero bytes standing for the coinbase (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like a sealed envelope stapled to the cover of a report: the pages inside can be checked against the seal, and the seal itself is listed on the cover.

nodes.label: Coinbase data and tags
nodes.body: The free data of the coinbase script is where pools sign their blocks: block 840,000 contains /ViaBTC/ and 'Mined by buzz120', block 709,632 contains /F2Pool/ and block 277,316 contains /P2SH/, and the scripts have 96, 100 and 15 bytes, all within the limit of 2 to 100 bytes (Mempool Space, 2026); (Mempool Space, 2026). The limit is enforced: a test block with a one-byte script and one with 101 bytes were both refused with bad-cb-length (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book says that miners use this space for extra nonce values and strings identifying the mining pool (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). That is how the statistics of pools in this chapter can be made at all, by reading the tags. It is like the stamp of a printer in the corner of a poster: nobody requires it, but it tells you who made it. nodes.label: The extra nonce changes the root
nodes.body: The coinbase is the first leaf of the merkle tree, so any change to its script changes its identifier, then every hash above it up to the merkle root in the header, and so the hash of the whole header (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). On the test chain two blocks that differed only in an extra nonce in the coinbase script and had the same header nonce gave different coinbase identifiers, different merkle roots and different block hashes (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This is the extra-nonce trick: when the 4-byte nonce runs out, the miner changes the extra nonce and starts over on a completely different header. It is like changing one word in the first line of a letter that is sealed with a wax stamp built from all lines: the stamp for the whole letter is new.

nodes.label: Header construction
nodes.body: This section is about the 80-byte header that is hashed: its fields in a real block, the version bits and the two rules for the time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This subject covers Header of block277316; Version history; Median time past; Two hour rule.

nodes.label: Header of block277316
nodes.body: The book builds its mining example on block 277,316 and gives its target, 0x0000000000000003A30C followed by zeros (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); the 80-byte header of that block can be taken apart: version 2, the hash of the previous block, the merkle root c91c008c..., the time 1388185914, the bits 1903a30c and the nonce 924591752. Parsed from the saved copy, the time is 2013-12-27 23:11:54 UTC, the merkle root equals the one listed by mempool.space, the double SHA-256 of the 80 bytes is the block hash 0000000000000001b6b9a13b095e96db41c4a928b97ef2d944a9b31b2cc7bdc4, and that hash is below the target of the bits (Mempool Space, 2026); (Mempool Space, 2026). Anyone with the 80 bytes can repeat the check in a few lines. It is like checking a lottery ticket against the published winning numbers: you need only the ticket and the list. nodes.label: Version history
nodes.body: The first field of the header was meant as a version number but became a bulletin board: block 277,316 has the version 2 of BIP 34, block 709,632 has 0x20200004, and block 840,000 has 0x2a5fe000 (Mempool Space, 2026); (Mempool Space, 2026). BIP 9 requires the top three bits to be 001 for blocks that signal for a soft fork, so every version from 0x20000000 on follows its pattern, and bit 2 of block 709,632 is the signal for taproot (Wuille et al., 2015); (Wuille et al., 2020). In block 840,000 the lower bits 0x0a5fe000 are no signal but data that mining hardware rolls, as BIP 320 allows (BtcDrak, 2018). The book says that the use of the field has changed over time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like a form whose 'title' box has been used for years as a free note field: the old meaning is still printed, the actual meaning is whatever the writers agree on. nodes.label: Median time past
nodes.body: The timestamp in a header is written by the miner and cannot be proven, so the rules bound it: a block must be later than the median of the previous 11 blocks, a value called the median time past, and BIP 113 uses the same median for lock times (Kerin and Friedenbach, 2015). The test chain refused a block whose time was equal to the median with the reason time-too-old, and Bitcoin Core's chain code defines the median by taking the middle of the last 11 timestamps (Bitcoin Core, 2026). For block 277,316 the median time past was 2013-12-27 22:34:35 UTC, and the block's own time was 2,239 seconds later; the book states the rule as 'no node will accept a block with a time less than or equal to the median time of the last 11 blocks' (Mempool Space, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like a witness who is believed if his clock is no earlier than what most of the previous eleven witnesses said: one liar cannot pull the median. nodes.label: Two hour rule
nodes.body: The other bound on a timestamp is to the future: a node does not accept a block more than two hours ahead of its own clock, which Bitcoin Core writes as MAX_FUTURE_BLOCK_TIME = 2 * 60 * 60 seconds, 7,200 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A test block whose time was two hours and a second ahead was refused with time-too-new (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The two bounds together keep the time in a window, which matters because the time sets the difficulty; the book gives the reason that a miner could otherwise lower difficulty by lying about the time (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Optech's topic on the time warp attack explains what happens when these bounds are bent: the median time past then increases much more slowly than normal (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). It is like a rule that an exam may not be started earlier than the invigilator's clock allows, nor claimed to have started more than two hours late.

nodes.label: Proof of work
nodes.body: The fourth subject is the work itself: a hash below a target, a target that follows from a compact number, and a difficulty that adjusts every 2,016 blocks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The retarget rule reproduced a real adjustment of 2024 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This subject covers The lottery; Target and difficulty; Retargeting.

nodes.label: The lottery
nodes.body: This section is about the idea of proof of work shown with a toy hash, a pair of dice and the cost of checking compared to the cost of finding (Back, 2002). This subject covers The Hello World nonce; Dice analogy; Proof is cheap to check.

nodes.label: The Hello World nonce
nodes.body: The book explains proof of work with a toy: add a counter, the nonce, to the phrase 'Hello, world!' and hash until the result starts with a zero (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The first counter that works is 32, whose hash begins 09cb91f8, exactly as the book prints; two zeros first appear at 228 and three zeros at 3,460, each roughly 16 times harder. The book's prose writes the phrase 'Hello, World! 32' with a capital W, which gives a different hash (6bbe6a3d), while its shell example uses a lowercase w: a typing slip, shown by the recomputation. The idea is older than Bitcoin, from Back's Hashcash and the pricing function of Dwork and Naor (Back, 2002); (Dwork and Naor, 1992). It is like asking a friend to spin a roulette wheel until a zero comes up: a quick spin for a green zero is luck, and the number of spins is the proof of effort.

nodes.label: Dice analogy
nodes.body: The book compares the hunt for a hash to a game with two dice, in which the players throw until someone gets a throw less than a target, and a lower target makes winning harder (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The numbers can be counted: of the 36 possible throws of two dice, 3 are at most 3 (8.33%), 6 are at most 4 and 26 are at most 8, so the odds fall as the target falls. A hash does the same with a number of 256 bits instead of 36 outcomes: the target is the threshold, and the proportion of hashes that win is the target divided by 2 to the 256 (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). It is like a fairground game where the prize is on a shelf that gets higher each week: the throw is the same, the chance is smaller.
nodes.example: the dice game with a target
nodes.definition: In the dice game of the book a throw of two dice wins if it is at most the target: the target 3 wins in 3 of 36 throws (8.33%), 4 in 6 of 36 and 8 in 26 of 36, so a lower target means a harder win, as with a hash.

nodes.label: Proof is cheap to check
nodes.body: Proof of work is expensive to produce and cheap to check, the property that makes it useful (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). On the Bitcoin Core 31.1 test chain a search for a hash below the target with bits 1e0fffff took 1,031,915 attempts, near the expected 1,048,577, and a search at 1f00ffff took 72,470 against 65,537 expected, while the regtest target needed one; each winning hash was confirmed by a single comparison (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The first scheme of this kind to price a resource by computation was proposed by Dwork and Naor, and Back's Hashcash used hash prefixes for the same purpose before Bitcoin; Nakamoto's paper cites Hashcash (Dwork and Naor, 1992); (Back, 2002); (Nakamoto, 2008). It is like a jigsaw puzzle: finding the solution takes an evening, but a guest sees at a glance that it is finished.
nodes.example: 1,031,915 hashes to find, one to check
nodes.definition: Finding a hash below a target takes many attempts and checking it takes one: on the test chain the search at bits 1e0fffff needed 1,031,915 attempts (expected 1,048,577), at 1f00ffff 72,470 (expected 65,537) and at regtest difficulty 1, and the winning hash was verified by one comparison.

nodes.label: Target and difficulty
nodes.body: This section is about the target, the way it is packed in the header, the difficulty and the hash rate that follows from it (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). This subject covers Hash below target; Difficulty from target; Compact bits; The wait of a terahash miner; Hash rate from difficulty.

nodes.label: Hash below target
nodes.body: A block is valid proof of work if the number that is its header hash, read as a 256-bit integer, is not above the target written in its header, which means that the hash must start with many zero bits (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Block 277,316 had a target that fits in 194 bits, so a winning hash needed at least 62 leading zero bits; its hash 0000000000000001b6b9a13b... has 63, and the book says 'more than 60' (Mempool Space, 2026). The check is one double SHA-256 and one comparison, as the saved header showed. It is like a high-jump bar set at a fixed height: the jumper is judged only by whether he cleared it, and the judge needs a second to see. This example reads mempool_header_277316.txt, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.14.6 and not in your browser: (63, 194, 62, True, '0x3a30c00000', True)
nodes.definition: Block 277,316 had to hash below a target of 194 bits, so its hash needed at least 62 leading zero bits, and it has 63, hash 0000000000000001b6b9a13b...; the book says 'more than 60'.

nodes.label: Difficulty from target
nodes.body: Difficulty is a more convenient name for the same thing: the ratio of the largest allowed target, the one with the bits 0x1d00ffff and difficulty 1, to the target of the block (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). For block 277,316 with bits 1903a30c this gives 1,180,923,195, the same figure as mempool.space lists, and for block 840,000 it gives 86,388,558,925,171, about 73,000 times harder (Mempool Space, 2026); (Mempool Space, 2026). The book writes the target as a long hexadecimal number and the difficulty as its reciprocal in disguise (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like the handicap in golf: the same course, but each year the par is made smaller and the number that says how much smaller is the difficulty. This example reads mempool_block_277316.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.14.6 and not in your browser: (1180923195, 1180923195, 1.0, 86388558925171, 86388558925171, True)
nodes.definition: Difficulty is the ratio of the easiest target (0x1d00ffff, difficulty 1) to the block's target: bits 1903a30c give 1,180,923,195 for block 277,316, equal to what mempool.space lists, and block 840,000 had 86,388,558,925,171.

nodes.label: Compact bits
nodes.body: A target has 256 bits but the header has room for only 4 bytes, so it is stored in a compact form: one byte of exponent and three bytes of mantissa, with the target equal to the mantissa times 256 to the power of the exponent minus 3 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The code of Bitcoin Core turns a target into this form with a function named GetCompact (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Block 277,316 has bits 0x1903a30c, which is 0x03a30c times 256 to the power 22; converting back gave 0x1903a30c, the value 0x1d00ffff expanded to the difficulty-1 target, and a mantissa with its high bit set, 0x00800000, was shifted to 0x04008000 because that bit is a sign bit. It is like writing a big number in scientific notation, 3.2 x 10^22, to fit a small box on a form: three digits and the position of the point. This example reads mempool_block_840000.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.14.6 and not in your browser: ('0x3a30c00000000000000000000000000000000000000000000', '0x1903a30c', '0x4008000', '0xffff0000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000', True, True)
nodes.definition: The 4-byte bits field stores a target as an exponent byte and three bytes of mantissa: 0x1903a30c is 0x03a30c times 256 to the power 22, converting back gives 0x1903a30c, a mantissa with its high bit set is shifted (0x00800000 becomes 0x04008000) and 0x1d00ffff expands to the difficulty-1 target.

nodes.label: The wait of a terahash miner
nodes.body: The book works out how long a single machine would take: a miner doing 1 TH/s, one trillion hashes per second, would find a block for height 277,316 'once in 8,496 blocks or once every 59 days' (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Recomputed, the expected number of hashes is the difficulty 1,180,923,195 times 2 to the 32, so at 10 to the 12 per second it takes 58.7 days, which is 8,453 blocks of ten minutes, about 0.5 percent fewer than the book's figure; 8,496 blocks of ten minutes are 59.0 days, so the number of blocks and the number of days of the book agree with each other and not with the difficulty (Mempool Space, 2026). It is a small slip, but a good habit for a reader: the figure can be recomputed with two lines. It is like a bus timetable that says 59 minutes when the clock on the route says 58.7: fine for a traveller, wrong for an engineer.
nodes.definition: The book says that one miner doing 1 TH/s would find a block of height 277,316 once in 8,496 blocks or 59 days; the difficulty 1,180,923,195 times 2 to the 32 divided by 10 to the 12 gives 58.7 days or 8,453 blocks, about 0.5% fewer.

nodes.label: Hash rate from difficulty
nodes.body: Nobody measures the hash rate of the network directly; it is estimated from the difficulty, because difficulty times 2 to the 32 hashes is the expected work for a block and a block comes every 600 seconds (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). The difficulty of the last retarget, 132,716,002,350,731, gives 9.5e20 hashes per second, 8 percent under the 1.029e21 that mempool.space reports from recent blocks and near the 1.003e21 of blockchain.com; the two services estimate over different windows (Mempool Space, 2026); (Blockchain Charts, 2026). The network is therefore about 121,738 times faster than the 8.45e15 that the difficulty of block 277,316 implied in 2013, when the book's example was chosen. It is like estimating the traffic of a city from the number of tickets sold: you do not count every car, you count what is needed to explain the numbers. nodes.label: Retargeting
nodes.body: This section is about the adjustment every 2,016 blocks, tested against a real epoch, with its flaws, its limits and its newest branch (Bitcoin Core, 2026). This subject covers Retarget formula on real epoch; The 2015-gap retarget; The factor-of-four clamp; Regtest never retargets; The BIP 94 branch; Recent adjustments; Next adjustment today.

nodes.label: Retarget formula on real epoch
nodes.body: Every 2,016 blocks the network resets the target so that the next 2,016 blocks should take two weeks, 1,209,600 seconds: the new target is the old one multiplied by the time the last period took and divided by two weeks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The rule was applied to real headers: block 838,656 and block 840,671 are the first and the last of a period and 1,186,047 seconds apart; with the bits 17034219 of the last block the function gives 170331db, which is the value that block 840,672 really carries, so the code reproduces the network to the last digit (Mempool Space, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026). That period was 1.02 times faster than planned, so the target fell by 2 percent and mining became 2 percent harder. It is like a thermostat that is set after each fortnight: if the room warmed up faster than planned, the heater is turned down a little. nodes.label: The 2015-gap retarget
nodes.body: The retarget has a small famous flaw: it measures the time from the first to the last block of the period, which is 2,015 intervals and not 2,016, so the intended pace is a block every 599.7 seconds instead of every 600 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The ratio 2016 divided by 2015 is 1.000496, or 0.05 percent faster than the aim, and the code takes the first block at height minus 2,015 and subtracts its time from that of the last block (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book's listing of the code shows the same arithmetic without naming the effect (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like a fence with 2,016 posts that has only 2,015 gaps between them: if you plan the length with the wrong count, the fence is a little off.
nodes.definition: The timespan is measured from the first to the last block of a period, which are 2015 gaps and not 2016, so the retargeting aims at a block every 9.995 minutes, 0.05% faster than 10; the code takes the first block as height minus 2015 and the difference of the last block's time.

nodes.label: The factor-of-four clamp
nodes.body: The measured time of a period is limited to between a quarter and four times the aim before it is used, so that the target can change by at most a factor of four at a retarget, in either direction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the recomputation a period ten times too long gave a target exactly 4 times larger (bits 170d0864 from 17034219) and a period ten times too short gave 0.25 times (1700d086), and the two lines of pow.cpp that apply the limits were found in the source (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The limit protects against a wild estimate after a sudden loss of most of the hash rate, though it also means that recovery can take several periods. It is like a car with a speed limiter on the gas pedal: however hard you push, the speed changes only so fast.

nodes.label: Regtest never retargets
nodes.body: The regtest chain switches the difficulty adjustment off with a parameter, fPowNoRetargeting, which is true for regtest and false for mainnet in chainparams.cpp (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The test chain of this chapter was mined through heights 1, 2015, 2016, 2017 and 2100 and the bits stayed 207fffff throughout, so a real retarget by Bitcoin Core was not executed; the retarget function was instead checked against real mainnet headers. Release 29.0 also turned off the timewarp rule of BIP 94 on regtest (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025). It is like practising a free kick without a wall: the ball goes in, but the real difficulty has been switched off.

nodes.label: The BIP 94 branch
nodes.body: The listing of the retarget code in the book is an older version, and the file pow.cpp of Bitcoin Core 31.1 has an extra branch, if (params.enforce_BIP94), which builds the new target from the bits of the first block of the period instead of the last, because the first block is not allowed to use the minimum-difficulty exception and so keeps the real difficulty, as a comment in the code explains (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The flag is true for testnet4 and false for mainnet, and the word enforce_BIP94 does not occur in the book (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). BIP 94, assigned on 2024-05-27, describes the rules, among them the 'Time Warp Attack Prevention' (Jahr, 2024). It is like the extra clause that a contract acquires after a dispute: the old text is still there, and the new clause applies only to one customer.

nodes.label: Mining competition
nodes.body: The fifth subject is the contest among miners: how they get enough room to vary the header, how they join in pools, and how large a share of the hash rate would be needed to attack (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The statistics come from the blocks of the last year (Mempool Space, 2026). This subject covers Nonce space; Mining pools; Hashrate attacks.

nodes.label: Nonce space
nodes.body: This section is about running out of nonces and the three ways round it: the extra nonce, the rolled version bits and the tricks of the hardware (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This subject covers The nonce space is tiny; The extra nonce space; Version rolling; Covert ASICBoost.

nodes.label: The nonce space is tiny
nodes.body: The nonce of the header is 4 bytes, so a miner can try 4,294,967,296 values before the header is used up and a new one is needed (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The network now runs at about 1.029e21 hashes per second, which uses up 2 to the 32 values in 4.17 picoseconds and means that the network works through 2.4e11 whole nonce spaces every second (Mempool Space, 2026). That is why a single nonce cannot keep a machine busy and miners need more room in the header to vary. The book dates this problem to the arrival of ASICs, when hardware exceeded 4 GH/s and then 1 TH/s (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like a car's trip counter with only four digits on a lorry that drives a million kilometres: the counter rolls over faster than anyone can read it. nodes.label: The extra nonce space
nodes.body: The first solution was to use the coinbase script as extra room: eight bytes of extra nonce added to the 4-byte nonce give 2 to the 96 possible headers, a number the book writes as 8 followed by 28 zeros (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Calculated exactly, it is 7.923e28 and has 29 digits, so the book's rounded form is right, and 2 to the 64 times 2 to the 32 equals 2 to the 96. Because the coinbase is the first leaf of the merkle tree, each new extra nonce means recomputing the left side of the tree up to the root, which the book calls more complicated for equipment and protocols than changing only the header (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like a lock with a second dial added to the first: the combinations multiply instead of adding.
nodes.definition: An 8-byte extra nonce in the coinbase and the 4-byte nonce give 2 to the 96, 7.9e28, headers to try without touching the timestamp, a number with 29 digits that the book writes as 8 followed by 28 zeros.

nodes.label: Version rolling
nodes.body: The solution of the machine makers is to roll 16 bits of the version field, the mask 0x1fffe000 of BIP 320, which gives 65,536 versions for each coinbase (BtcDrak, 2018). Together with the 2 to the 32 nonces this is 2 to the 48 hashes per header, so one machine can run at 281.5 TH/s if it finishes a header every second, the 281 TH/s of the book (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). On the test chain a block with the rolled version 0x2000e000 was accepted at height 3 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Pool protocols carry the same idea: BIP 310 adds a 'version-rolling' extension to Stratum so that the machine may roll these bits without asking the pool (Palatinus et al., 2017). BIP 320 has the status Draft, although it is widely used, and BIP 323 was proposed as its replacement. It is like a combination lock with sixteen free switches on the side: the machine can flip them without changing the keys of the lock.

nodes.label: Covert ASICBoost
nodes.body: ASICBoost is a technique for constructing the block header specially so that the hardware does less work per hash (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). The book tells that segwit unintentionally interfered with covert ASICBoost, so that miners who used it would lose their hidden advantage if segwit were activated, and that this conflict of interest became part of the dispute over activation in 2017 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The segwit commitment sits in the coinbase, where BIP 141 requires it (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The case is a good lesson that a technical rule can change the profit of a group of miners, and the miners then take a side. It is like a new traffic rule that happens to ban the shortcut that only some drivers knew: they will have views on the rule.
nodes.definition: Covert ASICBoost is a hidden hardware shortcut in the search for a hash; the book recounts that segwit interfered with it, so that miners who used it would have lost their advantage if segwit were activated, which is one reason given for the dispute of 2017.

nodes.label: Mining pools
nodes.body: This section is about pools: how concentrated they are, why small miners join, how shares are counted, which protocols they speak and what attacks them (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This subject covers Pool concentration; Solo miner variance; Pool shares and fees; Stratum protocols; Block withholding.

nodes.label: Pool concentration
nodes.body: Most miners do not mine alone but in pools, which add the work of many machines and share the rewards, so that the identity of the finder of a block says who runs the largest pools (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). In the 52,371 blocks of the last year, Foundry USA found 14,750 (28.2 percent), AntPool 9,510 (18.2), F2Pool 6,602 (12.6) and ViaBTC 5,077 (9.7), so the two largest pools together found 46.3 percent and the four largest 68.6 percent, from a list of 32 named pools (Mempool Space, 2026). A pool is a manager of machines and not the owner of all of them, and the machines may leave for another pool, but the concentration is the first number to look at when asking how far the network is from the thresholds of attack. It is like a few big wholesale markets that supply many small stalls: the stalls are many, but the trucks start from a few gates. This example reads mempool_pools_1y.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. nodes.definition: In the last year, of 52,371 blocks, Foundry USA mined 14,750 (28.2%), AntPool 9,510 (18.2%), F2Pool 6,602 (12.6%) and ViaBTC 5,077 (9.7%), so two pools found 46.3% and four 68.6% of the blocks, out of 32 named pools.

nodes.label: Solo miner variance
nodes.body: The book says that a miner with 1 percent of the network hash rate would find more than one block per day on average (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); with 144 blocks a day this is 1.44 blocks. A miner with 0.01 percent would find 5.26 blocks per year, would wait 69 days on average between blocks, and would see no block in a whole year with a probability of 0.52 percent, but in any single month the chance of no block is 65 percent, because the waiting time is exponentially distributed. That variance is why small miners join a pool and accept a smaller, steady income and a fee of the manager in place of a rare large prize. It is like fishing alone with one line or in a fleet that shares the catch: the fleet's income is stable, the loner's depends on one lucky day.
nodes.example: 1% of the hash rate, 1.44 blocks a day
nodes.definition: A miner with 1% of the hash rate would average 1.44 blocks a day, as the book says (more than one), but one with 0.01% averages 5.26 blocks a year, waits 69 days on average, and has a 0.52% chance of seeing none in the year, which is why small miners join pools.

nodes.label: Pool shares and fees
nodes.body: A pool needs a way to see that its members really work, so it asks for shares: hashes that are below an easier target than the network's, and a member proves effort by showing many of them (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). If one hash in 1,024 is a share, a miner expects 1,024 shares for each hash that would win a block, and the chance of finding at least one share in 1,024 tries is 63 percent, as the arithmetic shows; the book's own count for a pool is typically more than 1,000 shares per block, with managed pools taking a percentage fee for the service, and P2Pool as the decentralized alternative (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Different pools pay by different rules, for example pay per share or pay per last N shares (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). It is like a collective that pays pickers by the full baskets they hand in, although only one in a thousand baskets contains the golden strawberry.
nodes.definition: A pool sets an easier target so that members prove their work with shares: with one in 1,024 hashes being a share, a miner expects a thousand shares for each block, and the pool pays by the share and takes a fee.

nodes.label: Stratum protocols
nodes.body: A pool and a machine speak a protocol, and the usual one is Stratum, which has been used since 2012 for pooled mining and replaced the older getwork (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). BIP 310 extends it with a 'version-rolling' feature, and the RPC getblocktemplate of BIP 22 is the other way a miner obtains work from a node (Palatinus et al., 2017); (Dashjr, 2012). Stratum V2 is a binary protocol that encrypts the channel and optionally lets miners declare their own block templates, so that the pool does not choose every transaction, and Bitcoin Core 30.0 added an experimental IPC mining interface to work with Stratum v2 or other client software (Stratum contributors, 2026); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025). The book says that pool miners connect to the pool server using Stratum, version 1 or version 2, and that in version 1 the pool builds the candidate header and sends it to its miners as a template (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). No pool session was run for this chapter. It is like the difference between a delivery company that picks your route and one that lets you plan your own: the packages are the same, the control is not. This example reads stratum_v2_specification.txt, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. nodes.label: Block withholding
nodes.body: A pool has an attack against it that the book's pool section does not mention: a member submits shares and is paid for them, but never submits a share that would be a full block, so the pool gets none of the block rewards he finds (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). The Optech topic estimates that such a miner keeps 99.9 percent of the expected revenue without doing any good for the pool, and it names oblivious shares as a proposed remedy. The case shows that a pool depends on trust and on what it can verify. It is like a pickers' collective in which one member hands in only the unripe fruit and keeps the ripe fruit for himself.
nodes.example: a pool member who hides the winner
nodes.definition: A member of a pool can hand in shares but keep back a block that would win, damaging the pool without gaining a reward; Optech describes the attack and the book's pool section does not.

nodes.label: Hashrate attacks
nodes.body: This section is about the attacks that need a large share of the hash rate and how likely they are to succeed at each share (Nakamoto, 2008). This subject covers Nakamoto's catch-up odds; The selfish-mining threshold; The top pool against the thresholds; The limits of a majority attack.

nodes.label: Nakamoto's catch-up odds
nodes.body: Nakamoto's paper computes the chance that an attacker with a share q of the hash rate ever catches up from z blocks behind, a Poisson sum that falls fast with z when q is under one half (Nakamoto, 2008). Recomputed, a 10 percent attacker has a chance of 0.0002428 from 6 blocks behind, the value printed in the paper, and 0.2045873 from one block; a 30 percent attacker has 0.1321 from 6 blocks and a 45 percent attacker 0.766, while a half-share attacker is nearly sure to win, which is why the book advises more confirmations for large amounts (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Rosenfeld extends the analysis to the case where the merchant waits for a number of confirmations (Rosenfeld, 2014). It is like a race where the runner who is behind by 6 laps needs a long run of luck to catch up, unless he is nearly as fast as the leader.
nodes.definition: An attacker with 10% of the hash rate catches up from 6 blocks behind with probability 0.0002428 and from 1 block with 0.2045873; with 30% the figure for 6 blocks is 0.1321, with 45% it is 0.766 and with half it is nearly certain, recomputed with Nakamoto's formula.

nodes.label: The selfish-mining threshold
nodes.body: Selfish mining is a strategy in which a miner keeps found blocks secret and releases them to waste the work of others; Eyal and Sirer show that it pays above a threshold that depends on the share g of honest miners who follow the selfish block, and that the upper bound of the threshold is 1/3 of the network (Eyal and Sirer, 2013). The threshold is (1 - g) / (3 - 2g): one third when g is 0, one quarter when g is one half, and nothing when g is 1, as the formula gave in the recomputation. Optech summarises that it allows a miner with less than a majority to earn more than his share (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). It is like a card player who hides cards up his sleeve and shows them at the right time: only if enough of the table believes him does the trick pay. nodes.label: The top pool against the thresholds
nodes.body: Putting the numbers together: the largest pool of the last year, Foundry USA, found 28.16 percent of the blocks, below the one third of the strongest selfish-mining threshold but above the one quarter of its middle case, and the two largest pools found about 46 percent (Mempool Space, 2026); (Eyal and Sirer, 2013). A pool's share of blocks is not the share of an owner, since members can leave, so the figures say how concentrated the coordination is and not that the attack is likely; the book itself notes that the consensus depends on a majority of the miners acting honestly in their own interest (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like the largest party in a parliament that has under a third of the seats: not a majority, but enough that others must listen. nodes.definition: The largest pool of the last year, Foundry USA, found 28.16% of the blocks, under 1/3 and over 1/4, and the two largest together 46%.

nodes.label: The limits of a majority attack
nodes.body: A majority attack, usually called a 51 percent attack, lets a group with most of the hash rate build a private chain longer than the public one and publish it, so that its own earlier payments disappear (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026). The book states what the attacker can do: double-spend his own transactions and censor chosen transactions by re-mining any block that includes them; and it adds that the attack does not actually require 51 percent but only becomes almost certain there (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The recomputed odds agree: 45 percent has a chance of 0.766 from 6 blocks behind, and 50 percent is above 0.99. No attack on a public chain was run for this chapter; only the private double spend of the reorganization leaf. It is like a person who owns most of the votes in a club: he cannot forge another member's signature, but he can outvote everybody on what the minutes say.
nodes.definition: The book says that a majority attacker can double-spend his own transactions and can censor chosen transactions by re-mining blocks that include them, and that the attack can be attempted with less than 51%; the odds computed above agree.

nodes.label: Changing consensus rules
nodes.body: The sixth subject is how the rules can be changed without breaking the network: hard forks that need everybody and soft forks that need only the miners, with the signalling schemes that decide when (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The deployments were followed on real blocks and in state machines run on test chains (Wuille et al., 2015). This subject covers Hard forks; Soft forks.

nodes.label: Hard forks
nodes.body: This section is about changes that split the network: the arithmetic of a minority chain, the accidental fork of 2013 and the deliberate fork of 2017 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This subject covers The minority chain is slow; The chain split of March 2013; The Bitcoin Cash fork of 2017.

nodes.label: The minority chain is slow
nodes.body: In a hard fork, nodes with new rules accept blocks that the old nodes reject, and the two groups follow different chains (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's example of an 80 to 20 split gives the arithmetic: the 80 percent chain gets a block every 12.5 minutes, so 2,016 blocks take 25,200 minutes, 17.5 days, before its difficulty drops, while the 20 percent chain gets a block every 50 minutes and needs 70 days for a retarget. A fork where the minority chain is that slow will probably wither, which is one way in which hard forks end. It is like a road that splits where 80 of 100 cars take the left branch: the right branch is almost empty, and almost no one uses it a week later.
nodes.definition: If 80% follow new rules after a hard fork, their chain gets a block every 12.5 minutes and needs 17.5 days (25,200 minutes) for 2016 blocks before the difficulty drops, while the 20% chain gets a block every 50 minutes and needs 70 days.

nodes.label: The chain split of March 2013
nodes.body: The book mentions in a single sentence the unanticipated hard fork of the upgrade from Bitcoin Core 0.7 to 0.8, caused by a limitation of the Berkeley DB used to store blocks (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); the dates and numbers are as follows. The fork happened on 2013-03-11 at 23:24:19 UTC, when block 225,430, a block with 797 transactions and 249,119 bytes, was accepted by Bitcoin 0.8 and rejected by older versions (Mempool Space, 2026). BIP 50 explains why: versions before 0.8 had too few Berkeley DB locks to process a large but valid block, which made the lock limit an accidental consensus rule, while 0.8 used LevelDB and did not have that limit (Andresen, 2013); (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). Vitalik Buterin reported for Bitcoin Magazine that for about six hours there were two networks with two histories, and the split lasted 24 blocks, which agrees with block 225,454 at 06:19:32 UTC the next morning (Buterin, 2013); (Mempool Space, 2026). The pools Slush and BTCGuild went back to 0.7 to restore the old chain, giving up some income (Andresen, 2013). It is like two railway lines that go to different stations because a switch was set differently in two depots. nodes.label: The Bitcoin Cash fork of 2017
nodes.body: A fork can also be made on purpose: Bitcoin Cash split from Bitcoin on 1 August 2017 at block 478,559, and the last block that both share is 478,558 (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). It changed the rules and kept the 2016-block difficulty adjustment but added an emergency adjustment, which is the kind of hard fork the book describes: nodes that do not upgrade cannot follow, and those that do end up on another chain (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The split happened a few weeks before segwit became active, on 24 August 2017 at block 481,824 (Wikipedia contributors, 2026). It is like a group of friends who agree to separate at a crossroads, and from then on neither can follow the other's route.

nodes.label: Soft forks
nodes.body: This section is about changes that keep old nodes on the chain, and the schemes used to decide when to switch them on: counting, BIP 9, BIP 8 and Speedy Trial (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This subject covers A soft fork only tightens; BIP 34 activation; The BIP 9 state machine; Failed deployment; Segwit activation in 2017; BIP 8 lock-in by height; Speedy Trial and taproot; Buried deployments; BIP 54 consensus cleanup.

nodes.label: A soft fork only tightens
nodes.body: A soft fork makes the rules stricter, so that blocks valid under the new rules are also valid under the old ones, and old nodes keep following the chain as long as a majority of the miners enforce the new rules (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The test pair of Bitcoin Core 31.1 nodes showed the asymmetry: a lax node accepted a block with no height in the coinbase while the strict node answered bad-cb-height, the strict node then could not follow the lax chain (prev-blk-not-found), and when the strict chain became longer the lax node reorganized onto it (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Both nodes rejected a block of version 1, which is rule BIP 34 in force. It is like a club that bans shorts: those in trousers are welcome in both the old and the new club, but someone in shorts can enter only the old one.

nodes.label: BIP 34 activation
nodes.body: BIP 34 was the first soft fork to be activated by counting the version of recent blocks: when 750 of the last 1,000 blocks were version 2 or greater, invalid version-2 blocks were refused, and when 950 of the last 1,000 were, all version-1 blocks were refused (Andresen, 2012). The book gives the same two thresholds (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The history is now written into the code as plain heights: BIP 34 applies from block 227,931 on mainnet and 21,111 on testnet3 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). On the test pair of nodes the strict node reported BIP 34 as buried and active from height 1. It is like a library that waits until three quarters of the members have the new card and then, when nearly all have it, stops accepting the old card. nodes.label: The BIP 9 state machine
nodes.body: BIP 9 replaced the counting of BIP 34 with a state machine for each deployment: defined, started, locked_in, active or failed, decided once per period of 2,016 blocks, with the threshold of 1,916 blocks (95 percent) and one of bits 0 to 28 to signal on (Wuille et al., 2015). The book shows the diagram and says that proposals that reach the threshold are activated one period later (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). On the Bitcoin Core 31.1 test chain, with a period of 144 and a threshold of 108, the deployment was defined at height 143, started at 144, locked_in at 288 and active at 432 (Bitcoin Core, 2026), and the node's source has the same state names (Bitcoin Core, 2026). It is like a bill in a parliament: introduced, voted on, approved and then in force after a waiting period.

nodes.label: Failed deployment
nodes.body: A proposal that does not get enough signals before its timeout is not shelved but marked failed, and stays failed for ever (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). On the test chain a deployment with the timeout 1 was defined at height 143, started at 144 and failed at height 288, at the end of the first period, and the block version the node itself produced stayed 0x20000000, signalling nothing (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The state machine is the one of BIP 9 (Wuille et al., 2015). Failure is part of the design: a change that the miners do not want does not take effect by accident. It is like a petition that closes on a set date: if it has too few signatures by then, it lapses and cannot be opened again.
nodes.definition: A deployment whose time ran out without enough signals goes from started to failed at the end of its period (height 288 in the test) and stays failed for ever.

nodes.label: Segwit activation in 2017
nodes.body: Segregated witness was proposed for activation with BIP 9 on bit 1 between 2016-11-15 and 2017-11-15, but it was not activated by miners for a long time (Hilliard, 2017). BIP 91 specified a method to activate it with a majority of hashpower below 95 percent, and BIP 148 a flag day on which nodes would reject blocks that did not signal, which the book recounts as the proposal of a pseudonymous developer (Hilliard, 2017); (Shaolinfry, 2017); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The Wikipedia article states that blocks 477,792 to 479,807 signalled, locking it in, and that it was active on 24 August 2017 at block 481,824, the figure that chainparams.cpp gives, with CSV at 419,328 (Wikipedia contributors, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026). BIP 141 is also where the witness commitment explained earlier is defined (Lombrozo et al., 2015). It is like a strike notice that is withdrawn when the other side starts to talk: the deadline did its work without being used.

nodes.label: BIP 8 lock-in by height
nodes.body: BIP 8 is a redesign of BIP 9: it counts in block heights instead of time, and has a flag lockinontimeout which, if true, requires blocks to signal in the final period, so that the soft fork is locked in by the timeout height (Fry and Dashjr, 2017). The book explains that many users saw it as a flaw of BIP 9 that miners could prevent an activation by not signalling for a year, and that BIP 8 therefore defines a MUST_SIGNAL period in which miners must signal; software using it was published for taproot in 2021 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Optech's overview of soft fork activation lists the proposals and the debate (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). No node of this chapter ran BIP 8. It is like a deadline in a contract that says what happens if nobody signs: the default is no longer 'nothing'.
nodes.definition: BIP 8 counts in blocks and not in time, and has an option lockinontimeout that forces the lock-in at the end, a design made after the segwit episode.

nodes.label: Speedy Trial and taproot
nodes.body: Taproot was activated by a quick variant of BIP 9 called Speedy Trial: start 2021-04-24, timeout 2021-08-11, a threshold of 1,815 of 2,016 blocks (90 percent, instead of 1,916) and a minimum activation height of 709,632 (Wuille et al., 2020). Bitcoin Core 0.21.1 shipped these parameters, and the chain parameters of release 31.1 still carry them with bit 2 (Bitcoin Core developers, 2021); (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The first block under taproot rules, block 709,632, was mined by F2Pool on 2021-11-14 at 05:15:27 UTC (Mempool Space, 2026). Optech has a topic on taproot and its activation (Bitcoin Optech, 2026). It is like a trial period in a shop for a new till: if enough staff accept it within three months, it starts on the date after the next stocktake. This example reads mempool_block_709632.json, a file saved with the chapter's evidence that the page does not carry, a file whose terms of redistribution are not clear and which the page therefore does not carry. Recorded output, produced when the chapter was built under Python 3.14.6 and not in your browser: ('2021-04-24', '2021-08-11', 1815, 0.9003, True, 'F2Pool', '2021-11-14 05:15:27', '709632', True, True)
nodes.definition: Taproot was activated with Speedy Trial: start 2021-04-24, timeout 2021-08-11, a threshold of 1,815 of 2,016 (90%), and a minimum activation height of 709,632; block 709,632 was mined by F2Pool on 2021-11-14 05:15:27 UTC.

nodes.label: Buried deployments
nodes.body: When a soft fork is long past, the node no longer needs to count votes and writes down only its height: BIP 34, 65, 66 and CSV and segwit are in the chain parameters as heights, for example SegwitHeight 481,824 and CSVHeight 419,328 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The deploymentinfo source names them bip34, bip65, dersig, csv and segwit next to taproot and a test dummy, and on the two test nodes BIP 34 was reported as buried, active from height 1 on the strict node and at height 100,000 on the lax one (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026). BIP 65 (OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY) and BIP 66 (strict DER signatures) are among those soft forks, and both have the status Deployed in their documents (Todd, 2014); (Wuille, 2015). It is like a street that was once a building site: after it opens, the plan shrinks to a line on the map.

nodes.label: BIP 54 consensus cleanup
nodes.body: The next proposed change of the rules, BIP 54, the consensus cleanup, fixes the time warp attack, makes a transaction invalid if its inputs have more than 2,500 signature operations, forbids transactions of exactly 64 bytes without witness data, and sets the coinbase locktime to the height minus 1 (Poinsot and Corallo, 2025). Optech explains the time warp: miners can make a period look four weeks long and halve the difficulty (Bitcoin Optech, 2026), and Bitcoin Core 30.0 has a change made to prepare for a possible BIP 54 deployment in the future (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025). The same rules have a test network version in BIP 94 (Jahr, 2024). It is not active on mainnet, and the book, written in 2023, does not mention it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). It is like a spring clean of the rules: several small repairs bundled so that the cost of one change is shared.
nodes.example: a clean-up that is not yet active
nodes.definition: BIP 54, the consensus cleanup, proposes to fix the time warp attack, to invalidate a transaction with more than 2,500 signature operations over its inputs, to forbid transactions of exactly 64 bytes and to set the coinbase locktime to the height minus 1, but it is not active: the release notes of Bitcoin Core 30.0 speak of preparing for a possible BIP 54 deployment in the future.
