findings: Background

The chapter states that the reward halves every 210,000 blocks, from 50 coins in 2009 to 25 in 2012, 12.5 in 2016 and 6.25 in 2020 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The saved blocks confirm each date and reward: block 210,000 on 2012-11-28, block 420,000 on 2016-07-09, block 630,000 on 2020-05-11 and block 840,000 on 2024-04-20 at 00:09:27 UTC, the first to pay 3.125 coins, and the subsidy function of the node shifts the integer subsidy right once per interval (Mempool Space, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Background

The supply cannot exceed 21 million coins: the sum of the 33 non-zero rewards is 2,099,999,997,690,000 satoshis, 2,310,000 satoshis short of 21 million coins, and the last block with a reward of 1 satoshi is 6,929,999, which supports the book's 'approximately the year 2140' (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026).
Comparative analysis

The consensus checks are not only described but run: thirteen transaction cases and fourteen block cases on a Bitcoin Core 31.1 node each gave a named reason, apart from one transaction with no inputs that could not even be decoded (bad-txns-premature-spend-of-coinbase at depth 1 and 99 and success at 100, bad-cb-amount, bad-cb-height, bad-cb-length for 1 and 101 bytes, time-too-old, time-too-new, bad-txnmrklroot, high-hash, bad-diffbits, bad-blk-length), and the reasons are defined in the validation source (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

Chain selection is by cumulative work and not by length: on two test nodes a payment of 49.999 coins with one confirmation went to -2 confirmations when a competing branch with chainwork 208 against 206 replaced it, Carol had received 0 and the refund had 2 confirmations; the book's definition of the best chain as the one with the most cumulative proof of work agrees, and Rosenfeld's analysis gives the odds of such a reversal (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Rosenfeld, 2014).
Comparative analysis

Median time past and the two-hour rule are both enforced: a test block equal to the median was refused as time-too-old and one two hours and a second ahead as time-too-new, MAX_FUTURE_BLOCK_TIME is 2 * 60 * 60 in chain.h, and BIP 113 uses the median of the last 11 blocks; Optech notes that a time warp attack makes the median time past increase much more slowly than normal (Kerin and Friedenbach, 2015); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).
Comparative analysis

Mining pools have a concentration that the book could not know: in the last year, of 52,371 blocks, Foundry USA found 28.2 percent, AntPool 18.2, F2Pool 12.6 and ViaBTC 9.7, so four pools found 68.6 percent; the book's remark that a miner with 1 percent of the hash rate finds more than a block a day (1.44) is right, while one with 0.01 percent waits 69 days on average (Mempool Space, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

Hash rate has risen beyond the book's examples: the difficulty of 132,716,002,350,731 implies 9.5e20 hashes per second, mempool.space reports 1.029e21 and blockchain.com 1.003e21, which is 121,738 times the 8.45e15 implied by the difficulty of block 277,316, the block of the book's example (Mempool Space, 2026); (Blockchain Charts, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

The threshold of attack is lower than the book's headline: the book says that a '51% attack' does not need 51 percent, and the paper on selfish mining proves that the upper bound of the threshold is one third, with one quarter for a pool whose blocks are followed by half of the honest miners; Nakamoto's own table gives 0.0002428 for a 10 percent attacker 6 blocks behind, which was recomputed, and Optech summarises selfish mining (Eyal and Sirer, 2013); (Nakamoto, 2008); (Bitcoin Optech, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

The book does not discuss block withholding, an attack against pools in which a member is paid for shares but never submits a share that would be a full block and keeps 99.9 percent of his expected revenue; Optech names oblivious shares as a proposed remedy, and Stratum V2, which lets miners declare their own templates, changes who chooses the transactions (Bitcoin Optech, 2026); (Stratum contributors, 2026); (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026).
Comparative analysis

Changed ecosystem: Bitcoin Core 30.0 added an experimental IPC mining interface that lets a node work with Stratum v2 or other client software, started with -ipcbind and the bitcoin command; the 31.1 help lists no -ipcbind option for bitcoind itself, so the interface was not executed here (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026).
Comparative analysis

The chain split of March 2013 is mentioned by the book in one sentence; the saved data give its numbers: block 225,430, 797 transactions and 249,119 bytes, at 2013-03-11 23:24:19 UTC, and a split that lasted 24 blocks to block 225,454 at 06:19:32 UTC the next morning, caused by the Berkeley DB lock limit of versions before 0.8; the pools of Slush and BTCGuild went back to 0.7 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Andresen, 2013); (Buterin, 2013); (Mempool Space, 2026).
Comparative analysis

The 80 to 20 hard-fork arithmetic of the book is right: 12.5 minutes per block and 25,200 minutes, 17.5 days, for 2,016 blocks on the 80 percent chain, and 50 minutes per block and 70 days on the 20 percent chain; the Bitcoin Cash split of 1 August 2017 at block 478,559 is an intended example (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Wikipedia contributors, 2026).
Comparative analysis

Soft forks were recomputed on test nodes: a lax node accepted a block with no height in the coinbase that a strict node refused with bad-cb-height, the strict node could not follow the lax chain, and the lax node reorganized onto the longer strict chain; BIP 34 itself counted 750 and 950 of 1,000 blocks, the numbers of the book, and is now a height in the code, 227,931 on mainnet (Andresen, 2012); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

BIP 9 is confirmed in a state machine run on the test chain: with a period of 144 and a threshold of 108 the deployment was defined at 143, started at 144, locked_in at 288 and active at 432, and a deployment with a timeout went to failed; the mainnet threshold is 1,916 of 2,016, on bits 0 to 28, and the node's source names the same states (Wuille et al., 2015); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

Activation methods after BIP 9 are in the chain data: segwit was activated on 24 August 2017 at block 481,824 after BIP 91 and BIP 148 were proposed; BIP 8 adds a lock-in by height; Speedy Trial for taproot opened on 2021-04-24, timed out on 2021-08-11 with a threshold of 1,815 of 2,016 and a minimum activation height of 709,632, and block 709,632 was mined by F2Pool on 2021-11-14 (Hilliard, 2017); (Shaolinfry, 2017); (Fry and Dashjr, 2017); (Wuille et al., 2020); (Mempool Space, 2026); (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).
Comparative analysis

The book was written before the consensus cleanup of BIP 54, which would fix the time warp attack, make a transaction invalid if it has more than 2,500 signature operations over its inputs, forbid transactions of exactly 64 bytes, and set the coinbase locktime; it is a proposal, and the release notes of Bitcoin Core 30.0 say that a change was made to prepare for a possible deployment (Poinsot and Corallo, 2025); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025); (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).
Conclusion

The idea of proof of work is older than Bitcoin and the book's toy example comes from it: Dwork and Naor proposed pricing functions against junk mail in 1992, Back proposed Hashcash in 1997 and wrote it up in 2002, and Nakamoto's paper cites Hashcash; the Bitcoin Wiki says that all Bitcoin miners create hashcash proofs of work (Dwork and Naor, 1992); (Back, 2002); (Nakamoto, 2008); (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026); (Wikipedia contributors, 2026).
Conclusion

Taken together, the chapter's account of mining, verification and the changing of rules stands, and nearly every claim could be recomputed. What is wrong or out of date lies at the edges: one float division in the supplied script, one capital letter, one ratio of blocks to days, the comfortable remark on fees, the old retarget listing and the field of the coinbase, and what has changed since the book is the concentration of the pools, the hash rate, the block reserved weight, the IPC mining interface and the proposed consensus cleanup (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Erratum of the book's code: max_money.py divides the reward with current_reward /= 2, a float division in Python 3, and run as printed it goes on for 1,107 steps and prints 2100000000000000.0 and not the 2099999997690000 of the text; with the integer division the book's figure appears (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Contemporary developments

Erratum of spelling: the book's toy proof of work says that 'Hello, World! 32' produces the hash 09cb91f8..., but the hash with a capital W is 6bbe6a3d...; the shell example in the same section uses a lowercase w, gives the printed hash and finds its first zero at the counter 32 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Contemporary developments

Erratum of arithmetic: the book says that at the difficulty of block 277,316 a miner doing 1 TH/s would find a block once in 8,496 blocks or 59 days; the difficulty 1,180,923,195 times 2 to the 32 divided by 10 to the 12 gives 58.7 days or 8,453 blocks, about half a percent fewer, and the hash of the block, with 63 leading zero bits, agrees with the book's 'more than 60' (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Mempool Space, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Changed state: the book says that fees are usually a small percentage of income, but block 840,000, mined by ViaBTC, paid 3,762,561,499 satoshis in fees against a subsidy of 312,500,000, 12.04 times as much, in 3,050 transactions; the claim is a description of the period of writing and not a law, and the book itself says that fees will matter more as the reward falls (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Mempool Space, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Changed default: the coinbase transaction made by Bitcoin Core 31.1 has nLockTime equal to the height minus 1, nSequence 0xfffffffe and a script that ends with OP_0, none of which is in the book's table; the locktime rule is the one of BIP 54 and keeps new coinbases different from the early violations of BIP 34 (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Poinsot and Corallo, 2025); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Contemporary developments

Changed default: since release 29.0 the block reserved weight is a single option, -blockreservedweight, default 8,000 weight units (the fixed 4,000 had been reserved twice by a bug), so a Bitcoin Core template never exceeds 3,992,000; block 840,000 weighed 3,993,281, so it was made by other software, and release 29.0 also stopped applying the BIP 94 timewarp mitigation on regtest (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Mempool Space, 2026).
Contemporary developments

The retarget rule of pow.cpp reproduces the real adjustment of 2024: from the headers of blocks 838,656 and 840,671, 1,186,047 seconds apart, and the bits 17034219, it computes 170331db, the bits of block 840,672; the 2,015-gap measurement makes the aim 0.05 percent faster than 10 minutes, and the clamp to a quarter and four times the two weeks works as recomputed (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Mempool Space, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Changed code: the book's listing of the retarget function has no branch for testnet4; Bitcoin Core 31.1 has if (params.enforce_BIP94), true for testnet4 and false for mainnet, which builds the new target from the bits of the first block of the period, because that block may not use the minimum-difficulty exception (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Jahr, 2024).
Contemporary developments

The version field is no longer a version: block 277,316 has 2, block 709,632 has 0x20200004 (bit 2 signals taproot) and block 840,000 has 0x2a5fe000, with rolled bits 0x0a5fe000 inside the mask 0x1fffe000 of BIP 320, a draft for which BIP 323 is proposed as replacement; 65,536 values times 2 to the 32 nonces give the 281 TH/s of the book, and a block with a rolled version was accepted on the test chain (BtcDrak, 2018); (Mempool Space, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

stories.who: Adam Back, the cryptographer who proposed Hashcash, Cynthia Dwork and Moni Naor, who proposed pricing functions against junk mail, and Satoshi Nakamoto, who cites Back's idea

stories.story: Proof of work did not start with Bitcoin: Cynthia Dwork and Moni Naor proposed in 1992 that a user should compute a moderately hard function before using a shared resource, to fight junk mail. Adam Back proposed Hashcash in 1997 and described it more formally in a paper dated 1 August 2002, in which the sender hashes a string with a growing counter until the hash begins with enough zeros. Nakamoto's paper says that Bitcoin needs a proof-of-work system similar to Adam Back's Hashcash. In this chapter the book's toy version, the phrase Hello, world! with a counter, found its first zero at 32, as the book prints, and a block of Bitcoin does the same with 62 or more zero bits.
stories.lesson: A cheap check of an expensive search can price any request

stories.who: Gavin Andresen, who wrote the post-mortem BIP 50, Marek Palatinus (Slush) and Michael Marsee (Eleuthria of BTCGuild), whose pools downgraded their nodes, and Vitalik Buterin, who reported it for Bitcoin Magazine

stories.story: On 11 March 2013 at 23:24:19 UTC block 225,430, with 797 transactions, was mined and accepted by nodes of Bitcoin 0.8 but rejected by some older nodes. BIP 50, written by Gavin Andresen, explains that versions before 0.8 had too few Berkeley DB locks for a large but valid block, which had accidentally become a rule of consensus, while 0.8 used LevelDB. Marek Palatinus and Michael Marsee downgraded their pools to 0.7 so that the old chain would carry the most work, and the split lasted 24 blocks, about six hours, until block 225,454. Most large businesses shut their deposits to protect themselves from double spends, which shows what the choice of the chain with most work means for a shop.
stories.lesson: An accident in software can become a rule of the network

lecture.title: Chapter 12: Mining and Consensus
lecture.say: This deck explains mining and consensus: the reward and its halving, the checklists that every node runs on a block, the nonce lottery of proof of work and its retargeting, the pools and attacks that follow, and the soft forks that change the rules. Every example runs under Python 3.14.6 on the chapter's own library, and Bitcoin Core 31.1 was run on a test network, so its answers are Recorded and only read back here. The research package for chapter 12 holds the sources and the claims.
lecture.takeaway: How new coins are made, how every node checks a block, why proof of work is a lottery, and how the rules change. Bitcoin Core 31.1 results are Recorded.

lecture.title: Today's route
lecture.say: The route has three parts after the questions: rewards, rules and the block, with the subsidy, the checklists, the chain of most work and the coinbase; proof of work, with its lottery, difficulty and retargeting; and competition and rule changes, with pools, attacks and forks. Each part carries a true story or a correction of the book that a reader can check on the slide. The numbers in the list let a reader jump straight to a part.
lecture.takeaway: Three parts, four true stories, and a list of what was not run

lecture.title: The questions this chapter answers
lecture.say: The chapter asks two questions that this deck answers by computation: which of its statements can be checked, and what has changed since print. The three numbers are counted from the research package, which holds 91 sources, 27 findings and 69 executed claims. Each slide that follows shows the computation behind one claim.
lecture.takeaway: Its own competency questions, and the numbers behind the answers

lecture.title: Rewards, rules and the block
lecture.say: This part is about money and rules. It starts with the subsidy that halves every 210,000 blocks and the fees that are added to it, then follows the checklists that every node runs on a transaction and a block, the rule that the chain with the most work wins, and the special first transaction of a block, the coinbase. The story of the part is the block in which fees beat the subsidy twelve times.
lecture.takeaway: Where new coins come from, who may claim them, and the rules a block must pass.

lecture.title: Halving and the 21 million limit
lecture.say: The subsidy is 50 coins shifted right by one bit for every 210,000 blocks, and four real blocks show it: 25, 12.5, 6.25 and 3.125 coins. Summed in whole satoshis the 33 non-zero rewards stop 2,310,000 satoshis short of 21 million coins, and the last reward of one satoshi is in block 6,929,999, about the year 2140. The book's script has an error: its float division makes Python 3 print 2100000000000000.0 and not the figure of the text.
lecture.takeaway: The reward halves every 210,000 blocks, so supply stops just below 21 million

lecture.title: A block's reward is subsidy plus fees
lecture.say: A block may claim at most the subsidy plus the fees of its transactions. The test node's template paid 345,369 satoshis, made of the subsidy and 40,194 of fees; a block that claimed one satoshi less was accepted and one that claimed one satoshi more was refused as bad-cb-amount. In block 840,000 the fees were 12.04 times the subsidy, which makes the book's remark that fees are usually a small percentage of income a description of its time and not a law.
lecture.takeaway: Reward is subsidy plus fees, and fees can be 12 times the subsidy

lecture.say: Block 840,000 was mined by ViaBTC at 00:09:27 UTC on 20 April 2024 and was the first to pay the new subsidy of 3.125 coins. Its 3,050 transactions paid 3,762,561,499 satoshis in fees, 12.04 times the subsidy, so the reward of 4,075,061,499 satoshis was made mostly of tips. The coinbase carries the tag /ViaBTC/, which is how the statistics of pools are made. The book says that fees are usually a small percentage of income, and this block is an exception.
lecture.takeaway: The story of 20 April 2024: who, where, when and what to read next

lecture.title: Node checklists for transactions and blocks
lecture.say: Consensus is a set of checks, and each one has a name. On a Bitcoin Core 31.1 test node, fourteen transaction cases and fourteen block cases each produced one reason: a repeated input, a negative output, a coinbase spent before 100 blocks, a reward one satoshi too high, no height in the coinbase, a wrong merkle root, a time not above the median or two hours ahead, and a version 1. The one valid block was accepted.
lecture.takeaway: Every rule has a name, and a node reports the first one a block breaks

lecture.title: The best chain has the most work
lecture.say: A node follows the chain with the most cumulative proof of work, which is not always the longest. On two test nodes a branch with chainwork 208 replaced one with 206, and a payment of 49.999 coins that had one confirmation went to minus two, so the receiver held nothing until the payment was mined again. The losing branch stays on record as a valid fork. The blocks were handed over by RPC and not relayed over the network.
lecture.takeaway: The chain with the most work wins, and a payment can fall back to zero

lecture.title: Coinbase fields and reserved weight
lecture.say: The first transaction of a block, the coinbase, has no real input. Since BIP 34 its script begins with the height, so block 2,204 starts with 029c08, and the coinbase of Bitcoin Core 31.1 also sets its locktime to the height minus one, its sequence to 0xfffffffe and ends the script with OP_0, none of which is in the book's table. Core now reserves 8,000 weight units for it, so its blocks stay below 3,992,000, and block 840,000 with 3,993,281 came from other software.
lecture.takeaway: The coinbase begins with the height; Core reserves 8,000 weight units for it

lecture.title: Proof of work
lecture.say: This part explains proof of work. It starts with a toy lottery in which a counter is hashed until the result is small enough, then asks how small the target must be and how much work that means in days. It ends with the rule that sets the target every 2,016 blocks, and with the story of Adam Back's Hashcash, from which the idea comes.
lecture.takeaway: A lottery whose odds the network sets, and a thermostat that keeps it fair.

lecture.title: Proof of work is a nonce lottery
lecture.say: Proof of work is a lottery in which anyone can check a winning ticket at once. In the book's toy version the phrase Hello, world with a counter first gives a hash that starts with a zero at 32; two zeros took 228 tries and three took 3,460. The book prints the phrase with a capital W, and that spelling gives a different hash, 6bbe6a3d; only the lowercase one gives 09cb91f8. Nothing was mined on a public network.
lecture.takeaway: A hash below the target is a winning ticket that anyone can check

labels.text: mining on the public network or with ASICs

lecture.title: Difficulty, hash rate and a 1 TH/s miner
lecture.say: Difficulty tells how many hashes a block takes on average: difficulty times 2 to the 32. At the difficulty of block 277,316, 1,180,923,195, a miner doing a trillion hashes a second needs 58.7 days, which is 8,453 blocks; the book says 8,496 blocks, an error of about half a percent. Today's hash rate, from the last adjustment and from mempool.space, is about 10 to the 21 per second, 121,738 times that of the book's example.
lecture.takeaway: At 1 TH/s a block takes 8,453 blocks of waiting, not the book's 8,496

lecture.title: Retargeting every 2,016 blocks
lecture.say: Every 2,016 blocks the target is scaled by the time the period took against two weeks, and never by more than a factor of four either way. From the headers of blocks 838,656 and 840,671, which are 1,186,047 seconds apart, the formula computes the bits 170331db, and that is what block 840,672 really carries. Counting 2,015 gaps and not 2,016 makes the aim 0.05 percent faster than ten minutes. Regtest does not retarget, so no real Bitcoin Core retarget was run.
lecture.takeaway: The formula reproduces a real adjustment; a swing is clamped to four times

labels.text: a real Core retarget; regtest never retargets, so the formula met real mainnet headers instead.

lecture.title: The BIP 94 branch and recent adjustments
lecture.say: The book's listing of the retarget function has no branch for testnet4, but Bitcoin Core 31.1 has one: when enforce_BIP94 is true, the new target is built from the bits of the first block of the period, which may not use the minimum-difficulty exception. It is true on testnet4 and false on the main chain. Regtest sets fPowNoRetargeting and keeps its bits forever. In the last two years there were 52 adjustments, from 0.888 to 1.147 times.
lecture.takeaway: Core has a BIP 94 branch that the book's retarget listing lacks

lecture.title: The stamp that made email cost something
lecture.say: Proof of work did not start with Bitcoin. Cynthia Dwork and Moni Naor proposed in 1992 that a user should compute a moderately hard function to fight junk mail, and Adam Back proposed Hashcash in 1997 and described it in a paper dated 1 August 2002. Satoshi Nakamoto's paper says that Bitcoin needs a proof of work similar to Back's Hashcash, and the book's toy search is the same idea in small.
lecture.takeaway: The story of 1 August 2002: who, where, when and what to read next

lecture.title: Competition and rule changes
lecture.say: This part is about competition and change. When the 32-bit nonce is used up a miner changes other fields, miners join pools to smooth their luck, and a pool with enough power can attack. Rule changes then come as soft forks, which only tighten, or hard forks, which split. The two stories are the chain split of March 2013 and the activation of taproot.
lecture.takeaway: What miners do when the lottery gets harder, how attackers fare, and how the rules change.

lecture.title: When the 32-bit nonce runs out
lecture.say: The nonce has only 4,294,967,296 values, and today's hash rate uses them up 240 billion times a second, so miners change something else. The extra nonce in the coinbase script changes the transaction id and the merkle root, which gives 2 to the 96 values. Version rolling lets miners also change 16 bits of the version, which gives 65,536 times as many nonces; on the test chain a block with a rolled version was accepted.
lecture.takeaway: A miner changes the extra nonce or the version bits when the nonce runs out

lecture.title: Mining pools: who finds the blocks
lecture.say: Mining by oneself is a lottery with long waits, so most miners join a pool that shares the reward by the shares of work each one sends. In the last year four pools found 68.6 percent of 52,371 blocks, with Foundry USA at 28.2 percent. The book's remark that a miner with 1 percent finds more than a block a day is right at 1.44, while one with 0.01 percent waits 69 days. No live pool or Stratum connection was made.
lecture.takeaway: Four pools found two thirds of the blocks; a small miner waits for months

lecture.title: How much power an attack needs
lecture.say: An attacker does not need 51 percent to do harm. Nakamoto's table gives a 10 percent attacker, six blocks behind, a chance of 0.0002428, and the chance grows fast with power: 0.1321 at 30 percent and 0.766 at 45 percent. The paper on selfish mining shows that a pool profits from hiding blocks above one third of the power, or one quarter if half of the honest miners follow its blocks, and the top pool holds 0.2816. No attack was run on a public chain.
lecture.takeaway: An attacker needs less than a majority; the top pool is below 1/3

labels.text: a 51 percent attack on a public chain

lecture.title: Soft forks tighten, hard forks split
lecture.say: A soft fork only tightens the rules, so old nodes still accept the new blocks; a hard fork loosens them and splits the chain. On two test nodes a lax node accepted a block with no height in its coinbase and a strict node refused it, and the strict node could not follow the lax chain. BIP 9 let miners signal in a window: with a period of 144 and a threshold of 108, the deployment went from defined to started, locked in and active. On the main chain the threshold is 1,916 of 2,016.
lecture.takeaway: A soft fork only tightens; BIP 9 lets miners signal, lock in and activate

lecture.title: The day Bitcoin had two histories
lecture.say: On 11 March 2013 a block of 797 transactions, number 225,430, was accepted by nodes of Bitcoin 0.8 and rejected by some older ones. BIP 50, written by Gavin Andresen, explains that versions before 0.8 had too few Berkeley DB locks for a large but valid block, which had become a rule by accident. The pools of Slush and BTCGuild went back to 0.7 so that the old chain had the most work, and the split lasted 24 blocks, about six hours.
lecture.takeaway: The story of 11 March 2013: who, where, when and what to read next

lecture.title: Taproot: a 90 percent vote on a clock
lecture.say: Taproot was activated by a variant of BIP 9 called Speedy Trial, which opened on 24 April 2021, timed out on 11 August 2021 and needed 1,815 of 2,016 blocks, 90 percent, instead of 1,916. It also set a minimum activation height of 709,632, so that nodes had time to upgrade. Block 709,632 was mined by F2Pool on 14 November 2021 with the version 0x20200004, in which bit 2 is the signal for taproot.
lecture.takeaway: The story of 14 November 2021: who, where, when and what to read next
